source.title: ParVL: Parallel Scaling and Expandable Compute Allocation for Multimodal LLMs
source.authors: Yang Yang; Qinyu Zhao; Mou-Xiang Chen; Xiao-Hui Li; Li-Xin Gu; Wen-Hai Wang; Hong-Jie Zhang; Wen-Wei Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplement are present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark scores across parallel-computation configurations in multimodal models, bearing on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit power laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling laws as background but does not test their loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute relationships. Its relevant results are benchmark scores under different branch-count configurations; it explicitly notes that these configurations do not isolate allocation under exactly matched compute. No rows are recorded for cited scaling-law findings or for efficiency measurements alone.
record.test_reason: The study cites scaling laws as background and evaluates its own parallel-computation method. Its branch-count sweeps measure benchmark gains and task-dependent allocation preferences, without testing a predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss. It reports no power-law fits, extrapolation tests, or compute-optimal parameter/token scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that shared-backbone parallel computation improves overall multimodal performance over same-recipe single-branch baselines, with task-dependent allocation preferences and modest gains at larger scales. They do not conclude that these results establish a predictive scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses parallel, parameter-shared ViT and LLM branches and full-parameter SFT, then evaluates multimodal benchmark scores. It does not reproduce the original held-out-loss scaling-law measurement or fit/extrapolation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark and domain scores vary with the ViT/LLM branch-count allocation. The authors report that allocations are not compared at exactly matched compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Parallel parameter reuse produces modest overall benchmark gains: 49.6 to 50.5 at 1B, 54.4 to 54.7 at 2B, and 62.5 to 63.0 at 8B. Preferred branch allocations differ by task, and some domain scores decrease. These are method-performance and allocation results without a tested scaling prediction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested InternVL3.5 SFT setting, expanding shared-backbone parallel computation can improve average multimodal benchmark performance, with task-dependent vision/language allocation preferences.

record.problems: Model-quality results use one training run per configuration, with no averaging across seeds. Training uses only a 1/20 subsample of one SFT collection and covers InternVL3.5 at 1B, 2B, and 8B; the authors note broader backbones, larger scales, and data-scaling experiments remain future work. Branch-count comparisons do not isolate allocation at exactly matched compute.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted within the retained aggregate metrics. Per-benchmark cells in Tables 1, 2, and S4 were not separately extracted; the catalog retains reported domain aggregates and the selected overall averages to represent downstream-score changes and allocation dependence.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute, including power-law form over orders of magnitude.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted to small runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed training compute and its scaling exponents. Vision/language branch allocation is a different allocation problem.
Loss sensitivity to architecture at fixed parameter count. Backbone parameters are shared, but total parameters vary and only downstream scores are reported.
Power-law form in multimodal training or SFT; neither setting alone establishes that form.
Predictable downstream improvement with scale or pretraining loss. The paper evaluates method gains at several backbone sizes and branch counts without evaluating a predictive scaling relationship.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token splits on setup and fitting choices, including departures from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: The recorded values and branch-count conditions agree with the supplied tables. Reference rows can remain as controls but cannot be classified as absent effects. Each quality result uses one training run, without seed replication. Unmatched compute prevents a fixed-compute allocation interpretation; this does not itself challenge V3 or V6.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute; no power-law fits.
No small-run fits or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute loss-minimising parameter/token allocation or scaling trend; branch configurations are not exactly compute-matched.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study is multimodal and uses SFT, but does not test whether a power-law loss form holds in these settings.
Tests benchmark performance across parallel-computation allocations in InternVL3.5 SFT models, not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or conventional parameter/token scaling.
No analysis of fitted scaling exponents, fitting choices, or curvature of loss-scaling curves.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected parallel configurations compared with same-recipe 1:1 baselines
reader_labels.reason: Overall scores rise from 49.6 to 50.1–50.5 at 1B, from 54.4 to 54.7 at 2B, and from 62.5 to 63.0 at 8B (r28-r31, r38-r39, r46-r47). These are benchmark gains, not evidence of power-law predictability.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Different branch allocations and benchmark domains
reader_labels.reason: Outcomes depend on task and allocation: General declines for several 1B allocations and at 2B, while Math/OCR often improve; no single configuration is best across tasks (r02-r27, r32-r37, r40-r45).
